Lessons.Title: Explaining Steps for Rewriting Equations
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning objective: explain why an algebraic move preserves solution sets or fails; identify equations with no solutions and avoid dividing by an expression that could be zero. Edulytiks original lesson aligned to Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 2 Lesson 7, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/2/7/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0), Addressing HSA-REI.A and HSA-REI.A.1. The source emphasizes oral arguments and critiques, not just computing x.

Original deliberate trap: x(x−4)=0 has solutions x=0 or x=4. Dividing both sides by x gives x−4=0, apparently leaving only x=4; the valid solution x=0 was lost because division by x is not allowed when x=0. Factoring and checking the zero-product property preserves both solutions. A second trap is x+2=x+5: subtract x to get 2=5, so it has no solution.

Partner reasoning task: assign one person a valid move (distributing, adding equal quantities, or dividing by a known nonzero constant) and the other an invalid move. Have each present a counterexample showing whether the entire original solution set is retained. Explain why x=0 cannot satisfy 6/x+1=8 because the original expression is undefined at zero.

Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, 8 max): correct original solution sets; explanation of valid moves; demonstration of division-by-variable pitfall; accurate no-solution and undefined-expression reasoning. It is not enough to record a final numeric value.

KeyConcepts.Title: Proof of equivalence
KeyConcepts.Definition: An algebraic transformation is valid when it preserves the full solution set.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Justify reversible moves or separately check lost cases.
KeyConcepts.Example: Dividing by a fixed nonzero number is reversible.

KeyConcepts.Title: Variable division risk
KeyConcepts.Definition: Dividing by an expression that may be zero can discard valid solutions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Split out zero cases before division.
KeyConcepts.Example: Dividing x(x−4)=0 by x discards solution x=0.

KeyConcepts.Title: No solution
KeyConcepts.Definition: An equation has no solution when every possible input yields a false equality.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find lost solution after division
WorkedExamples.Question: Analyze x(x−4)=0 and the move dividing by x.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use equivalence-preserving algebra, show domain restrictions and independently check a test value.
Steps: Zero-product property gives x=0 or x−4=0.
Division by x is undefined at x=0.
After dividing, equation x−4=0 keeps only 4.
Thus the equations are not equivalent.

WorkedExamples.Title: Recognize no solution
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve x+2=x+5.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use equivalence-preserving algebra, show domain restrictions and independently check a test value.
Steps: This is false for every real number.
Original equation has empty solution set.

WorkedExamples.Title: Separate undefined from false
WorkedExamples.Question: Can x=0 solve 6/x+1=8?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use equivalence-preserving algebra, show domain restrictions and independently check a test value.
Steps: At zero, division by zero is undefined, so substitution is not permitted.
WorkedExamples.Answer: x=6/7; zero is outside the domain.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Dividing through by x without checking zero
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: This eliminates x=0 if it was a solution.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Separate zero case or use factoring.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating undefined as a wrong numerical answer
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Division by zero is not a defined real calculation.

SummaryPoints: Equivalent equation steps must preserve ALL solutions.
Dividing by a possibly zero expression can lose solutions.
A contradiction like 2=5 proves there are no solutions.
Teacher evaluates the explanation or counterexample, not only the answer.

Visuals.Title: Original mathematically checkable table
Visuals.Description: Independent first-party numerical model; each row has an exact textual interpretation.
